top_cited_works.abstract: Abstract The development of a new class of multicomponent ultra‐high temperature ceramics (MC‐UHTCs), often referred to as high‐entropy UHTCs, has gained increased interest due to the possibility of improved thermomechanical and oxidation properties. In this study, a systematic approach by gradual addition in the UHTC components ranging from a binary to a dense quaternary (Ta,Nb,Hf,Ti)C is synthesized using spark plasma sintering (SPS). The solid solutioning was the critical factor in homogenizing the composition in the multicomponent system. The segregation of NbC and HfC was seen in binary and ternary UHTC systems, while a single‐phase homogeneity was observed in the quaternary UHTC improving its hardness up to 34.8 GPa. The presence of closely spaced slip lines in the MC‐UHTCs enhances resistance to indentation damage up to 72% at an applied load of 200 N. The formation of complex mixed oxide phase of Hf 6 Ta 2 O 17 ensued in the lower to negligible oxidation even up to 3 min of plasma exposure with temperature exceeding 2800°C. recent_works.title: Thermodynamic Pathways of Nonequilibrium Solidification in Wire‐Arc Additive Manufacturing Fe‐Based Multicomponent Alloy Structures
recent_works.abstract: Multicomponent alloys offer high strength, thermal stability, and corrosion resistance; however, their complex chemistries make phase formation under nonequilibrium additive manufacturing conditions difficult to predict. This study examines the thermodynamic pathways of an Fe‐based 140MXC multicomponent alloy fabricated by wire‐arc additive manufacturing (WAAM). Two geometries, a thin‐wall deposit (TWD) and a bulk‐wall deposit (BWD), were designed to impose distinct thermal gradients and reveal their influence on solidification. Multiscale microscopy, diffraction, and compositional mapping revealed that TWD exhibited strong heterogeneity, with refractory elements segregating to top layers and forming coarse NbC and W/Mo‐rich carbides due to reduced entropy stabilization. In contrast, BWD exhibited homogenized carbide distributions due to enhanced interlayer reheating, which stabilized mixing entropy and moderated segregation. Entropy calculations confirmed that decreasing entropic stabilization with cooling rate drives segregation–precipitation competition, consistent with Gibbs free energy predictions.
